← Back to the Facebook Marketplace fee calculator

How much does Facebook Marketplace take per sale?

Facebook Marketplace charges a 10% selling fee on a shipped checkout order, applied to the buyer-paid total -- the item price plus any buyer-paid shipping, and sales tax where Facebook collects it -- with an $0.80 minimum fee per sale. A sale arranged for local pickup instead carries no selling fee at all. The rate has changed more than once in the last two years, so a number quoted from an old blog post or forum thread may already be stale.

The shipped-order formula

fee = max(10% × (item price + buyer-paid shipping), $0.80)

payout = item price + buyer-paid shipping − fee − your own shipping-label cost

Local pickup skips the formula entirely: the fee is $0, so the payout is simply the item price minus whatever you spent on the item and packaging.

Worked example 1: $50 item, shipped, no buyer-paid shipping

LineAmount
Item price$50.00
Selling fee (10% of $50.00)$5.00
Payout$45.00

Worked example 2: the $0.80 minimum takes over on a small sale

LineAmount
Item price$5.00
10% of $5.00 would be$0.50
Selling fee actually charged ($0.80 minimum)$0.80
Payout$4.20

Not $4.50 (item price minus 10%) -- once the buyer-paid total falls under $8, the $0.80 minimum is the binding fee, not the 10% rate. This is the detail sellers who mentally calculate "just take 10% off" get wrong on small sales.

Shipping counts toward the fee base too

A $50 item with $10 in buyer-paid shipping pays 10% of the combined $60, which is $6.00 -- not 10% of the $50 item price alone. The payout is $54.00 ($60.00 collected minus the $6.00 fee), assuming you did not also pay for your own shipping label.

Local pickup: genuinely $0

LineAmount
Item price$50.00
Selling fee$0.00
Payout$50.00

No selling fee, listing fee, or subscription cost applies to a sale arranged for local pickup rather than Facebook's shipped checkout.

Do this with your own listings

The Facebook Marketplace fee calculator runs this same arithmetic on your own item price, shipping, and costs, flags when the $0.80 minimum is the binding fee, models a disputed order's flat $20 chargeback penalty, and solves for the price you need to hit a target profit. Nothing you type leaves your browser.

Common questions

How much does Facebook Marketplace take on a $50 sale?

For a shipped checkout order with no buyer-paid shipping: 10% of $50, which is $5.00, leaving a $45.00 payout.

How much does Facebook Marketplace take on a small $5 sale?

10% of $5 would be $0.50, but Facebook charges an $0.80 minimum fee on every shipped order, so the fee is $0.80, not $0.50 -- leaving a $4.20 payout instead of the $4.50 a flat 10% calculation would suggest.

How much does Facebook Marketplace take on a local pickup sale?

Nothing. Local pickup sales carry no selling fee, listing fee, or subscription cost -- the full item price is the payout, minus whatever you spent on the item and packaging yourself.

      Common questions

      How much does Facebook Marketplace take per sale?

      For a shipped checkout order, Facebook charges a 10% selling fee on the buyer-paid total -- the item price plus any buyer-paid shipping, and sales tax where Facebook collects it -- with an $0.80 minimum fee per sale. A locally arranged pickup sale has no selling fee at all.

      Is local pickup really free on Facebook Marketplace?

      Yes. Facebook does not charge a selling fee, listing fee, or subscription cost on a sale arranged for local pickup. The 10% fee only applies to orders that go through Facebook's shipped checkout.

      What is the $0.80 minimum fee?

      On a shipped order, if 10% of the buyer-paid total would come to less than $0.80, Facebook charges the $0.80 minimum instead. That only changes the fee on sales where the item price, shipping, and any tax collected add up to less than $8.

      What happens if a shipped order ends in a dispute?

      If a payment dispute on a shipped order is ruled against the seller, Facebook deducts a flat $20 chargeback penalty from the seller's payout ledger, on top of losing the sale itself. This tool models that as an optional toggle rather than assuming it by default.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

Facebook Marketplace Fee Calculator vs. doing the fee math by hand

Facebook's shipped-order fee is one rule with three exceptions: 10% of the buyer-paid total, an $0.80 minimum below an $8 total, and a $20 penalty on a disputed order. Holding all three in your head on every sale is where a mental estimate usually loses to a payout statement.

What mental math gets right, and what it drops

RuleDoing it by handThis calculator
10% shipped-order rateUsually rememberedApplied every time
Shipping and tax count toward the fee baseOften forgotten -- easy to fee only the item priceIncluded by default
$0.80 minimum below an $8 totalThe rule most often skipped entirelyApplied automatically, and flagged when it is the binding fee
$20 dispute penaltyRarely factored in until it happensAn explicit toggle
Price for a target profitRequires solving the fee formula backwards by handSolved directly, across the minimum-fee floor

A concrete example

A $5 item with no buyer-paid shipping: a mental estimate of "10% of $5" gives $0.50, and a payout of $4.50. The fee Facebook actually charges is the $0.80 minimum, since 10% of a $5 total falls short of it -- so the real payout is $4.20, thirty cents lower than the quick estimate. On a single sale that is small change; run the same shortcut across a weekend of listings and it adds up to a number a seller notices on the deposit.

Common questions

What does doing this math by hand usually miss?

Most often the $0.80 minimum fee on a small shipped sale -- 10% of a $5 total is $0.50, but the fee actually charged is $0.80, and a quick mental calculation defaults to the flat percentage. Buyer-paid shipping and any sales tax Facebook collected also count toward the fee base, not just the item price, which a mental estimate built around "10% of what I'm charging for the item" leaves out.

Isn't 10% simple enough to do in your head?

The percentage itself is simple. What is not simple in your head is remembering, on every single sale, to check whether the $0.80 minimum applies instead, whether shipping and tax belong in the base, and whether a dispute penalty changes the number -- four rules to hold at once rather than one.

When is doing it by hand the right call?

For a quick, rough estimate where being off by the price of a coffee does not matter. For pricing a listing to hit a specific take-home number, or checking a payout that already landed, the minimum-fee floor and the dispute penalty are exactly the kind of detail mental math drops first.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. Item prices, costs, and payouts are never uploaded, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your numbers.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, or selling advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. Verify every figure against Facebook's own Commerce/Seller Help pages or your own payout statement before pricing a listing.

← Facebook Marketplace fee calculator

Facebook Marketplace Fee Calculator vs. tracking sales in a spreadsheet

A seller who prices more than one Facebook Marketplace sale usually ends up with a spreadsheet: a cell for the 10% shipped rate, an IF formula for the $0.80 minimum on small sales, and a $0 row for local pickup. Each formula is ordinary arithmetic. Keeping the minimum-fee floor right, and rebuilding the target-profit formula each time the rate changes, is the part that gets skipped when a sale needs a price today.

What each approach actually does

A spreadsheet can reproduce every rate this calculator applies — the 10% shipped-order fee, the $0.80 minimum, and the $0 local-pickup fee. Building it means typing the right rate into the right cell, writing an IF formula for the minimum-fee floor, and writing your own formula to solve backwards for the price that hits a target profit. It also means noticing, on your own, when Facebook updates the rate.

This calculator keeps the shipped rate, the minimum-fee floor, and the $0 local-pickup fee on one screen, already wired to the current, corroborated rate, so a shipped sale and a local sale are the same worksheet instead of two. It solves backwards for the price that hits your target profit without a formula you have to write, correctly across the point where the minimum fee takes over from the percentage.

Common questions

Can a spreadsheet do this math instead?

Yes. The 10% shipped-order rate, the $0.80 minimum fee, and the $0 local-pickup fee are each ordinary arithmetic. Building it means typing Facebook's current rate into the right cell, adding an IF formula for the minimum-fee floor, and a second row for local pickup -- then remembering to update it the next time Facebook changes the rate.

What does a spreadsheet not do that this calculator does?

Keep the shipped rate, the $0.80 minimum, and the $0 local-pickup fee on one screen, already wired to the current, corroborated rate, so a shipped sale and a local sale are the same worksheet instead of two. It also solves backwards for the item price that hits a target profit without you writing that formula, across the minimum-fee floor where the relationship stops being a flat percentage.

Is a spreadsheet ever the better choice?

Yes, when your situation has a wrinkle this calculator does not model -- a bundle of several items in one order, a promotional credit, or a fee structure Facebook has changed since this tool's rate was last checked. A spreadsheet you build and update yourself can represent any rule you can describe. This calculator trades that flexibility for a form that already has the right fields for one item moving through Facebook's published shipped or local-pickup schedule.

Is my data uploaded anywhere?

No. The calculator runs entirely in your browser. Item prices, costs, and payouts are never uploaded, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your numbers.
